ch49.note: Yamazaki Susumu (died 1868) was a historical member of the Shinsengumi, an Osaka man who joined at the first recruitment and served as a kansatsu (inspector), the corps’s internal watch and intelligence arm. He is bound up above all with the Ikedaya affair of 1864, where by tradition he scouted the loyalist plotters. The Shinsengumi’s own records have him wounded at Toba-Fushimi and dying of the wounds aboard the Fujiyama-maru on the passage east, buried at sea as the novel describes; a few modern historians doubt the shipboard death, but it is the account Shiba follows.

ch49.anchor: the bond of this one meeting
ch49.note: An allusion to ichigo ichie (“one lifetime, one meeting”), a maxim of the tea ceremony holding that every gathering is unrepeatable and must be met as though it will never come again. Toshizō, an amateur of neither wealth nor leisure, reaches for the tearoom’s own idea of impermanence to say that a soldier can promise a woman nothing but the fullness of the present hour.

ch49.anchor: the hushed jakkō-light of the Buddha
ch49.note: Jakkō (寂光, “the light of quiescence”) is a Buddhist term for the serene radiance of enlightenment, and by extension of the Pure Land itself. The wordplay turns on two characters read shō: 照 (a hard, glaring “shining”) and 昭 (a soft “radiance”). The retreat is written Saishō-an with the gentler 昭, and Toshizō reads into it the quiet, valedictory glow of a setting sun rather than a blaze.

ch49.anchor: matsukaze, from Kameya Mutsu in Kyoto
ch49.note: Matsukaze (“wind in the pines”) is a flat, baked confection of wheat flour, malt syrup and white miso, poppy-seeds strewn on its glazed upper face and the underside left plain. It is the signature sweet of Kameya Mutsu, a Kyoto confectioner founded in 1421 that has long supplied the Nishi Hongan-ji temple; by the shop’s tradition the cake began as a siege ration during Oda Nobunaga’s decade-long war on the Ishiyama Hongan-ji (1570s) and took its name from a poem lamenting that hungry time. A Kyoto sweet, then, that carries the memory of a doomed defense: a pointed thing to set before this particular guest.

ch49.anchor: the resolute man never forgets that he may lie in a ditch
ch49.note: Toshizō is quoting Mencius (孟子, “Téng Wéng Gōng II”), who attributes the words to Confucius: the resolute officer never forgets that he may end in a ditch or gully; the brave officer never forgets that he may lose his head. The saying holds that a man of principle accepts from the outset an unhonored death, his corpse thrown in a gully and his severed head passing to the enemy. Its bleak fatalism suits Hijikata’s creed better than Kondō’s wish to be well buried.

Sendai-hira is a heavy, finely woven silk from Sendai, the most prized cloth for a samurai’s formal hakama (the pleated divided skirt). With a crested montsuki jacket it made the gravest ceremonial dress a man could wear; that Kondō rises from his sickbed to put it on marks how much weight he gives the naval funeral.

ch49.anchor: the anchorage off Tenpōzan at Osaka
ch49.note: Tenpōzan is a low artificial hill raised in 1831 from spoil dredged at the mouth of the Aji River, where it enters Osaka Bay; the deep water off it served as Osaka’s outer anchorage for seagoing ships, which could not ascend the shallow river to the city itself.

Shiba’s parenthesis is accurate. After Perry, the shogunate ordered in 1854 that Japanese ships fly the red sun-disc on white to distinguish them from foreign vessels, and used it as its own war-flag through Toba-Fushimi. It was the Restoration government that formally made the Hinomaru the national ensign, by the Commercial Shipping Regulations (Daijōkan Proclamation No. 57) of the first month of Meiji 3 (27 January 1870, old calendar); a separate proclamation that autumn fixed the naval flag. So in the First Month of Keiō 4, when Yamazaki is buried under it, the sun-disc is the shogunate’s flag, not yet by law the country’s.

Shinagawa was the first of the fifty-three post-stations of the Tōkaidō, the great highway between Edo and Kyoto, lying just south of Edo proper at the head of the bay. To come ashore there was, in effect, to arrive at the gate of Edo; it is a fitting first billet for a corps that has fought its way back from the capital it lost.

ch49.anchor: the shogunal Igakusho, the medical school by Izumibashi in Kanda
ch49.note: The Igakusho was the Tokugawa government’s school of Western (Dutch-derived) medicine, grown out of a vaccination clinic and by this date housed near Izumibashi in Kanda, Edo. Its director was Matsumoto Ryōjun, the bluff army-physician who has already tended Kondō and Okita at Osaka; it is to his institution that the two wounded men are carried ahead. It later became a root of the medical faculty of the University of Tokyo.

A kaimaki is a padded, kimono-shaped bedcover with sleeves and a collar, pulled over the sleeper like a wearable quilt; a single thin one, thrown over a man lying down in his clothes, is the barest sort of bedding, and the measure of how little comfort the corps now commands.
